chapters.headline: Measure space, without a ruler
points: The question: can counting events measure the size of a slice of space?
The paper is by T. Pierson (Axiovex Systems / Research, October 2026)
The article is the paper's 60-second explainer in full — video, text, and stills
chapters.takeaway: No ruler, no measuring rod — just events, links, and a count.

chapters.headline: Count the layers next to the slice
points: Spacetime as a sprinkling of events linked by cause and effect — the causal set picture
Count the last layer before the middle slice and the first layer after it
At a known sampling density, that count is a statistical ruler for the slice's area
chapters.takeaway: The count alone carries the size — no geometry is measured directly.

chapters.headline: The subtlety is the edges
points: The diamond narrows away from its middle, so a uniform formula expects too many counted events
The paper's fix is an exact finite-size correction — an accounting for the rim of the diamond
The corrected formula is a single exact prediction, not a fit
chapters.takeaway: Get the edges right, and the prediction is exact — derived, not tuned.

chapters.headline: A prediction that lands
points: With 2,000 events in the whole region: ignoring the edges predicts about 536 counted events
Including the correction predicts about 484 — the reported simulation average is 483, over 24 realizations
Across 4 model sizes and 72 simulations, the averages match the exact predictions within 0.8%
chapters.takeaway: Five hundred thirty-six without the correction; four hundred eighty-four with it; four hundred eighty-three measured.

chapters.headline: What this is, and what it is not
points: A better ruler for a model of spacetime — not a new law of gravity
The prediction was exact and made in advance; the correction was derived, not tuned
The reproducibility package (data + code) is public on Zenodo, and the Lean formalization is linked in the article
chapters.takeaway: Counting is a way of measuring — and the edges are the difference between a guess and a prediction that lands.
